learning_objective: 🎯 Understand how companies take massive public loans by issuing certificates of debt, and learn the rules for paying them back with interest!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Shareholders are owners who get 'Dividends' (if there is profit). Debenture holders are lenders (creditors) who get a fixed rate of 'Interest' strictly every year, even if the company suffers a loss.

Sometimes a company takes a bank loan and gives debentures to the bank as a secondary (backup) security. If the loan is paid, the debentures are returned. If the company defaults, the bank becomes a debenture holder.

Companies know the repayment terms on day one. If a company issues a debenture at ₹100 but promises to repay ₹110 after 5 years, they must immediately record the ₹10 future loss as 'Loss on Issue of Debentures'.
Redemption means paying the money back and canceling the debt. To protect investors, companies often have to create a DRR (Debenture Redemption Reserve) before paying them back.

fun_activity.title: 🤝 The Fixed IOU
fun_activity.instructions: Write an 'IOU' (I Owe You) note to your parents for ₹500. Write: 'I promise to pay 10% interest every year, and I will return exactly ₹550 after 2 years.' You just created a Debenture issued at par and redeemable at a premium!

exam_tips: 📌 Debenture Interest is a 'Charge against Profit', meaning it goes to the Statement of Profit & Loss (Finance Cost), NOT the Appropriation account. It must be paid even if the company is in loss.
📌 For 'Issue with Terms of Redemption' journal entries: ALWAYS credit 'Premium on Redemption of Debentures' and debit 'Loss on Issue' simultaneously when redeeming at a premium.
📌 Discount/Loss on issue of debentures must be written off in the VERY FIRST year itself from Securities Premium (if available) or Statement of P&L.
quick_recap: ⭐ Debentures carry a fixed rate of interest, which is a compulsory payment.
⭐ Debentures can be issued for cash, for consideration other than cash, or as collateral security.
⭐ The 'Premium on Redemption' is a liability representing the extra money the company promised to pay back in the future.
